passages.happening:
‘Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon, she came to test him with difficult questions’ (verse 1), with a great caravan of spices, gold and precious stones. Solomon answers all her questions (verse 2). When she sees his wisdom, his house, his table and his offerings, she is overwhelmed (verses 3-4).

She says, “The report I heard in my own country about your words and wisdom is true” (verse 5), and ‘You have far exceeded the report I heard’ (verse 6). She praises the LORD, ‘who has delighted in you to set you on His throne to be king for the LORD your God’ (verse 8), and says God made Solomon king ‘to carry out justice and righteousness’ (verse 8). She gives him gold and spices, he gives her all she asks, and she goes home (verses 9-12).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the summit and the end of Solomon's story in Chronicles. The wisdom God gave at Gibeon is known across the world, and a foreign queen says that Israel's God is its source.

Sheba is generally identified with Saba, a kingdom in south-western Arabia, modern Yemen, famous for frankincense, myrrh and spices carried north by camel along the incense routes. Its own inscriptions are mostly later than Solomon, and none names a queen of Sheba, so the visit is known only from the Bible and later traditions. The Ethiopian tradition that she bore Solomon a son, Menelik, is a medieval legend, not part of the biblical account. Visits between rulers, with rich gifts, were regular diplomacy and often had trade in view. Testing a ruler with riddles, chidot, was a known contest; wisdom was a mark of a true king.

The queen's words differ from Kings in one phrase. In 1 Kings 10:9 God set Solomon on the throne of Israel; here God set him on His throne. In Chronicles the throne is the LORD's, and the king rules for him. The pair justice and righteousness, mishpat and tsedaqah, names the heart of a king's calling.
passages.later: Jesus said, ‘The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here’ (Matthew 12:42).
passages.asks: The queen came a long way to test what she had heard, and found it more than true. Ask what you have heard about God that you have never tested for yourself. And ask whether people who watch your life would hear good report or bad.

passages.t: Gold, a throne of ivory, and Solomon's death
passages.happening:
Gold pours in each year, and Solomon makes shields of hammered gold and a great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and lions on each side (verses 13-19). ‘So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom’ (verse 22). ‘All the kings of the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart’ (verse 23). He has horses from Egypt and every land, and silver as common as stones (verses 25-28).

The rest of his acts are written ‘in the Records of Nathan the Prophet, in the Prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the Visions of Iddo the Seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat’ (verse 29). ‘Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years’ (verse 30), and he dies, and Rehoboam reigns in his place (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The chapter follows 1 Kings 10 closely, and its closing notice adapts 1 Kings 11:41-43, replacing Kings' one source with three prophetic records. The ivory throne with lions was a statement of royal power; lions were royal and divine symbols across the Near East, and ivory-inlaid furniture has been found in Assyrian palaces and at Samaria. The golden shields were for display in the hall called the House of the Forest of Lebanon, named for its rows of cedar pillars. They would not last: Shishak of Egypt carried them off in the next reign. The promise of riches and honor at Gibeon has been kept beyond measure. Then, abruptly, Solomon dies.

Who to notice: Ahijah the Shilonite in verse 29. He is the prophet who told Jeroboam that the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's son, and his name points to what Chronicles has not told.
passages.later: First Kings tells what Chronicles leaves out: ‘For when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been’ (1 Kings 11:4).
passages.hard:
Why does the Chronicler leave out Solomon's fall into idolatry?

First Kings 11 tells how Solomon's many foreign wives turned his heart to other gods in his old age, how God raised up adversaries against him, and how God announced that the kingdom would be torn from his son. Chronicles leaves all of this out and ends Solomon's reign at its height. Some readers see this as whitewashing.

Most interpreters see a deliberate focus instead. The Chronicler knew his readers had Kings. He does not deny Solomon's sins; he even points to them by citing Ahijah's prophecy in verse 29 and by opening chapter 10 with their consequences. His purpose was to present David and Solomon together as the founders of the temple and its worship, the model of Israel's life with God, for a community rebuilding that worship. Others note that the details of excess in this chapter, horses from Egypt and heaps of gold and silver, are exactly what the law for kings warned against, so an attentive reader can see the danger even here. Both readings take the text seriously: it celebrates what God gave and leaves the shadow in plain view for those who know the rest of the story.
passages.asks: The book ends Solomon's story at its height and lets the reader who knows Kings hear what is unsaid. Ask what gifts in your life have quietly become dangers. And ask how you want the story of your last years to be told.
